questions.stem: A worker’s average airborne exposure over a conventional 8-hour shift is being compared with an occupational limit. Which exposure metric is being used?
options: A ceiling limit, because it is averaged across the shift.
A short-term exposure limit, because the shift contains several tasks.
An IDLH concentration, because it applies to routine work.
questions.correctAnswerExplanation: A TWA weights each concentration by the time spent at that concentration and expresses the average exposure over the stated work period.
incorrectOptionExplanations: A ceiling is a concentration that should not be exceeded at any time; it is not an 8-hour average.
A STEL applies to a specified short averaging period rather than the full shift.
IDLH describes immediately dangerous conditions, not routine full-shift averaging.
questions.sourceTitle: Safety Professional's Reference and Study Guide, 4th ed. (W. David Yates, CRC Press, 2025)
questions.sourceLocation: Chapter 6, time-weighted average and exposure-limit concepts, pp. 240-243

questions.stem: A water-based cleaning concentrate has a very low pH and damages tissue on contact. Which description is most accurate?
options: It is automatically an oxidizer because every acid releases oxygen.
It is harmless after dilution with any amount of water.
It is a base because corrosive materials always have pH above 7.
It is acidic and may be corrosive; severity depends on concentration and the material’s other properties.
questions.correctAnswerExplanation: Low pH indicates acidity, and strong acids can cause corrosive tissue damage. pH alone should be considered with concentration, reactivity, and exposure conditions.
incorrectOptionExplanations: Acidity and oxidizing ability are different properties; not every acid is an oxidizer.
Dilution may reduce concentration, but it does not automatically eliminate hazard and may generate heat.
Corrosive materials can be strongly acidic or strongly basic.
questions.sourceTitle: Safety Professional's Reference and Study Guide, 4th ed. (W. David Yates, CRC Press, 2025)
questions.sourceLocation: Chapter 6, acids, bases, and pH, pp. 234-235

questions.stem: Why is molecular weight needed when converting a gas or vapor concentration between ppm and mg/m³ at a specified temperature and pressure?
options: It converts molar fraction to mass concentration, requiring molecular weight.
Molecular weight determines the sampling duration.
Molecular weight is used only to convert Celsius to Kelvin.
Molecular weight changes whenever the concentration changes.
questions.correctAnswerExplanation: For gases under specified conditions, ppm is a volume or mole fraction, while mg/m³ is a mass concentration. Molecular weight converts moles to mass.
incorrectOptionExplanations: Sampling duration affects collected volume but does not provide the mole-to-mass relationship.
Temperature conversion does not require molecular weight.
Molecular weight is a property of the substance and does not change with concentration.
questions.sourceTitle: Safety Professional's Reference and Study Guide, 4th ed. (W. David Yates, CRC Press, 2025)
questions.sourceLocation: Chapter 6, converting mg/m³ and ppm, pp. 245-246

questions.stem: Several solvents with similar toxic effects are each measured below their individual limits. What additional evaluation may still be necessary?
options: Ignore the mixture because every individual result is below its limit.
Sum each concentration-to-limit fraction to determine whether the combined additive exposure exceeds unity.
Add the numerical limits but not the measured concentrations.
Use only the chemical with the highest molecular weight.
questions.correctAnswerExplanation: When agents have similar additive effects, individual compliance does not ensure the mixture is acceptable. The exposure fractions are summed and compared with 1.0.
incorrectOptionExplanations: Several sub-limit exposures can combine to exceed an additive mixture criterion.
The evaluation must compare each measured concentration with its own limit.
Molecular weight alone does not identify the controlling combined toxic effect.
questions.sourceTitle: Safety Professional's Reference and Study Guide, 4th ed. (W. David Yates, CRC Press, 2025)
questions.sourceLocation: Chapter 6, gaseous mixtures and percentage of mixture limits, pp. 243-245

questions.stem: A tracer gas is present at 0.018% by volume. What is the concentration in ppm?
questions.correctAnswerExplanation: One percent equals 10,000 ppm. Therefore, 0.018% × 10,000 ppm/% = 180 ppm.
incorrectOptionExplanations: This uses 1% = 1,000 ppm instead of 10,000 ppm.
This is a factor-of-ten high conversion.
This moves the decimal in the wrong direction.
questions.sourceTitle: Safety Professional's Reference and Study Guide, 4th ed. (W. David Yates, CRC Press, 2025)
questions.sourceLocation: Chapter 6, concentrations of vapors, gases, and particulates, pp. 240-241

questions.stem: At 25°C and 1 atm, a toluene concentration is 185 mg/m³. Using a molecular weight of 92.14 g/mol, what is the approximate concentration in ppm?
incorrectOptionExplanations: This multiplies by molecular weight rather than dividing by it.
This divides by both molecular weight and molar volume.
This omits the molecular-weight divisor and applies only the molar-volume factor.
questions.sourceTitle: Safety Professional's Reference and Study Guide, 4th ed. (W. David Yates, CRC Press, 2025)
questions.sourceLocation: Chapter 6, converting mg/m³ to ppm, pp. 245-246
questions.formula: ppm = mg/m³ × 24.45 / MW at 25°C and 1 atm

questions.stem: At 25°C and 1 atm, a benzene concentration is 75 ppm. Using a molecular weight of 78.11 g/mol, what is the approximate concentration in mg/m³?
questions.correctAnswerExplanation: mg/m³ = ppm × MW / 24.45 = 75 × 78.11 / 24.45 = 239.6 mg/m³, which rounds to about 240 mg/m³.
incorrectOptionExplanations: This is a factor-of-ten low result.
This multiplies ppm by molecular weight but omits the molar-volume divisor.
This treats ppm and mg/m³ as numerically interchangeable.
questions.sourceTitle: Safety Professional's Reference and Study Guide, 4th ed. (W. David Yates, CRC Press, 2025)
questions.sourceLocation: Chapter 6, converting ppm to mg/m³, pp. 245-246
questions.formula: mg/m³ = ppm × MW / 24.45 at 25°C and 1 atm

questions.stem: A worker is exposed to 18 ppm for 2 hours, 8 ppm for 3 hours, and 2 ppm for 3 hours. What is the 8-hour TWA?
incorrectOptionExplanations: This takes a simple average of the three concentrations without weighting by time.
This omits or misweights one of the exposure periods.
This adds the concentrations without dividing by total time.
questions.sourceTitle: Safety Professional's Reference and Study Guide, 4th ed. (W. David Yates, CRC Press, 2025)

questions.stem: Three solvents with similar toxic effects are present at 40 ppm with a 100-ppm limit, 12 ppm with a 50-ppm limit, and 5 ppm with a 25-ppm limit. What is the additive mixture fraction?
questions.correctAnswerExplanation: Mixture fraction = 40/100 + 12/50 + 5/25 = 0.40 + 0.24 + 0.20 = 0.84. Because it is below 1.0, the additive criterion is not exceeded on these data.
incorrectOptionExplanations: This overstates one or more concentration-to-limit fractions.
This adds the concentrations and divides by a single limit, ignoring the separate limits.
This counts the number of chemicals rather than calculating exposure fractions.
questions.sourceTitle: Safety Professional's Reference and Study Guide, 4th ed. (W. David Yates, CRC Press, 2025)

questions.stem: A rigid 6.0-ft³ gas cylinder drops from 1,800 psia to 1,770 psia while temperature remains constant. Approximately what free-gas volume was released at 14.7 psia?
questions.correctAnswerExplanation: The pressure decrease is 30 psia. At constant temperature, released free-gas volume = cylinder volume × pressure drop / atmospheric pressure = 6.0 × 30 / 14.7 = 12.24 ft³.
incorrectOptionExplanations: This assumes the released free-gas volume equals the cylinder’s internal volume.
This multiplies cylinder volume by the pressure drop but omits division by atmospheric pressure.
This reverses the pressure ratio.
questions.sourceTitle: Safety Professional's Reference and Study Guide, 4th ed. (W. David Yates, CRC Press, 2025)
questions.sourceLocation: Chapter 6, Boyle’s law and referenced equations, pp. 235-248
questions.formula: Vfree = Vcylinder × ΔP / Patm, at constant temperature

questions.stem: A flexible gas bag occupies 2.5 m³ at 295 K. If pressure remains constant and temperature rises to 350 K, what volume will it occupy?
questions.correctAnswerExplanation: At constant pressure, V₂ = V₁T₂/T₁ = 2.5 × 350 / 295 = 2.966 m³, which rounds to 2.97 m³.
incorrectOptionExplanations: This reverses the absolute-temperature ratio.
This assumes volume does not change with absolute temperature.
This uses the temperature difference as a direct volume multiplier.
questions.sourceTitle: Safety Professional's Reference and Study Guide, 4th ed. (W. David Yates, CRC Press, 2025)

questions.stem: A 2.0-m³ vessel contains an ideal gas at 101.3 kPa and 298 K. Approximately how many kilomoles are present? Use R = 8.314 kPa·m³/(kmol·K).
incorrectOptionExplanations: This is a factor-of-100 high result.
This is a factor-of-ten high result.
This multiplies by temperature rather than dividing by RT.
questions.sourceTitle: Safety Professional's Reference and Study Guide, 4th ed. (W. David Yates, CRC Press, 2025)

questions.stem: A vapor mixture is 40% component A with an LFL of 2.5 vol% and 60% component B with an LFL of 4.0 vol%. Estimate the mixture LFL using Le Chatelier’s relation.
incorrectOptionExplanations: This is the simple weighted arithmetic average, not Le Chatelier’s reciprocal relation.
This adds the two component LFLs without weighting.
This reports the denominator of the reciprocal equation as the final LFL.
questions.sourceTitle: Safety Professional's Reference and Study Guide, 4th ed. (W. David Yates, CRC Press, 2025)
questions.sourceLocation: Chapter 6, lower flammability limit of mixtures, pp. 246-249

questions.stem: A substance has an occupational exposure ceiling limit. How should the exposure be managed?
options: Allow brief exceedances whenever the 8-hour average is below the ceiling.
Compare only the weekly average with the ceiling value.
Double the ceiling for any task lasting less than 15 minutes.
Control the task so the concentration does not exceed the ceiling during any part of the exposure period.
questions.correctAnswerExplanation: Unlike a TWA, a ceiling is intended to limit peak concentration and should not be exceeded at any time during the working exposure.
incorrectOptionExplanations: A ceiling is not averaged over the shift in that way.
A weekly average cannot determine compliance with a peak ceiling.
A ceiling does not automatically permit a twofold short-duration excursion.
questions.sourceTitle: Safety Professional's Reference and Study Guide, 4th ed. (W. David Yates, CRC Press, 2025)
questions.sourceLocation: Chapter 6, occupational exposure limits and time-weighted averages, pp. 240-243
